17.text: The electromagnetic spectrum is ordered by increasing wavelength as gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves, and radio waves.
The approximate wavelength of gamma rays is less than 0.01 nm.
The approximate wavelength range of X-rays is 0.01 nm to 10 nm.
The approximate wavelength range of ultraviolet radiation is 10 nm to 400 nm.
The approximate wavelength range of visible light is 400 nm to 700 nm.
The approximate wavelength range of infrared radiation is 700 nm to 1 mm.
The approximate wavelength range of microwaves is 1 mm to 1 m.
The approximate wavelength of radio waves is greater than 1 m.
The approximate frequency of gamma rays is greater than 3 × 10¹⁹ Hz.
The approximate frequency range of X-rays is 3 × 10¹⁶ to 3 × 10¹⁹ Hz.
The approximate frequency range of ultraviolet radiation is 7.5 × 10¹⁴ to 3 × 10¹⁶ Hz.
The approximate frequency range of visible light is 4.3 × 10¹⁴ to 7.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
The approximate frequency range of infrared radiation is 3 × 10¹¹ to 4.3 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
The approximate frequency range of microwaves is 3 × 10⁸ to 3 × 10¹¹ Hz.
The approximate frequency of radio waves is less than 3 × 10⁸ Hz.
Gamma rays have the highest relative energy.
X-rays have very high relative energy.
Ultraviolet radiation has high relative energy.
Visible light has medium relative energy.
Infrared radiation has low relative energy.
Microwaves have lower relative energy.
Radio waves have the lowest relative energy.
AM and FM radio and TV signals are applications of radio-wave broadcasting.
Cellular networks are an application of radio-wave mobile communication.
Radar detection and ranging are applications of radio waves.
Long-distance links are an application of radio-wave satellite communication.
Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are applications of radio waves for short-range wireless communication.
Radio telescopes are an application of radio-wave astronomy.
Microwave ovens heat food through water-molecule resonance.
Speed guns, weather radar, and aircraft detection are applications of microwave radar.
Microwave satellite communication uses uplinks and downlinks.
4G and 5G frequencies are applications of microwave mobile networks.
Wi-Fi provides wireless internet using microwaves.
Microwave links provide point-to-point communication.
TV and air-conditioner remotes use infrared radiation.
Thermal-imaging cameras use infrared radiation for night vision.
Infrared heaters and physiotherapy use infrared radiation for heating.
Weather forecasting uses infrared radiation for cloud and temperature mapping.
Infrared astronomy studies cool stars and dust.
Motion sensors and night cameras use infrared radiation for security.
Some infrared wavelengths are used in fibre optics.
Human vision uses visible light to see the world.
Cameras and smartphones use visible light for photography.
Some visible wavelengths are used in optical fibres.
Lasers use visible light for pointers, surgery, and industry.
LEDs and bulbs use visible light for illumination.
Visible-light spectroscopy is used for analysis of materials.
Monitors and televisions use visible light in display screens.
Ultraviolet lamps sterilize by killing bacteria and viruses.
UV water filters use ultraviolet radiation for water purification.
Ultraviolet markers on currency and documents help detect forgery.
Vitamin D is synthesized by ultraviolet radiation in human skin.
Ultraviolet fluorescence is used for security features and forensic science.
Ultraviolet astronomy studies hot stars.
Photolithography uses ultraviolet radiation in semiconductor manufacturing.
Ultraviolet radiation can cause sunburn and skin cancer.
X-ray radiographs image bones and the chest.
CT scans use X-rays for detailed body imaging.
X-rays are used for baggage scanning at airports and in security.
X-ray crystallography determines the structure of crystals and DNA.
X-rays detect cracks in metals in industry.
X-ray astronomy studies hot gases and black holes.
High-energy X-rays are used in radiation therapy for cancer treatment.
Gamma-ray radiotherapy kills cancer cells.
Gamma rays sterilize medical instruments and food.
PET scans and gamma cameras use gamma rays for diagnostic imaging.
Gamma rays are used for thickness gauging and weld inspection in industry.
Gamma-ray astronomy studies gamma-ray bursts and neutron stars.
Nuclear medicine uses radioactive tracers involving gamma rays.
Gamma rays are used for detecting nuclear materials in security.
Gamma rays have the highest frequency, greater than 3 × 10¹⁹ Hz.
Radio waves have the lowest frequency, less than 3 × 10⁸ Hz.
Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength, less than 0.01 nm.
Radio waves have the longest wavelength, greater than 1 m.
Gamma rays have the highest energy, given by E = hν.
X-rays are used in radiography and CT scans.
Gamma rays are used in radiotherapy, PET scans, and sterilization.
Ultraviolet radiation is used for sterilization, vitamin D production, and treating skin diseases.
Infrared radiation is used in physiotherapy and thermal imaging.
Visible light is used in laser surgery, endoscopy, and illumination.
Microwaves are used in diathermy for deep heating.
Radio waves are used in MRI through radio-frequency pulses.
Radio waves are used for radio, television, mobile communication, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth.
Microwaves are used for satellite communication, radar, 5G, and microwave links.
Infrared radiation is used in remote controls and short-range data communication.
Visible light is used in experimental Li-Fi and some optical fibres.
Ultraviolet, X-ray, and gamma radiation are not used for normal communication.
Radio waves are used for communication and radar in defence.
Microwaves are used for radar-based aircraft and missile detection and for jamming in defence.
Infrared radiation is used for night vision, heat-seeking missiles, and surveillance.
X-rays are used for baggage and cargo scanning in defence.
Gamma rays are used for detecting nuclear materials in defence.
Visible and infrared lasers are used for range finding, targeting, and directed energy.
Radio telescopes use radio waves to study pulsars and the cosmic microwave background.
Microwaves are used to study the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB).
Infrared astronomy studies cool stars, interstellar dust, and exoplanets.
Optical telescopes use visible light to study stars, galaxies, and planets.
Ultraviolet astronomy studies hot young stars and the interstellar medium.
X-ray astronomy studies black holes, neutron stars, and hot gas in clusters.
Gamma-ray astronomy studies gamma-ray bursts, supernovae, and active galaxies.

15.text: Silver has the lowest resistivity among conductors.
Silver is the best conductor.
Copper has excellent conductivity.
Copper is widely used in wires.
Aluminium is a good conductor.
Aluminium is lightweight.
Aluminium is used for power transmission.
Gold is an excellent conductor.
Gold is corrosion resistant.
Iron and steel are moderate conductors.
Graphite is a conductor among non-metals.
Electrolytes such as salt solution are ionic conductors.
Rubber has high resistivity.
Rubber is used for insulation.
Plastic is an excellent insulator.
Glass has very high resistivity.
Dry wood is a good insulator.
Mica is used in capacitors.
Mica is used for high-voltage insulation.
Ceramic is a high-temperature insulator.
Air and vacuum are natural insulators.
Dry paper is used in capacitors.
Silicon is an elemental semiconductor.
Silicon is the most widely used elemental semiconductor.
Germanium is an elemental semiconductor.
Carbon in the form of graphite is a special-case semiconductor.
Gallium arsenide is a compound semiconductor.
Cadmium sulphide is a compound semiconductor.
Selenium is an elemental semiconductor.
Lead sulphide is a compound semiconductor.
The atomic number of silicon is 14.
Silicon has 4 valence electrons.
Silicon has a diamond cubic crystal structure.
Silicon has a band gap of approximately 1.1 eV at room temperature.
Silicon has a higher band gap than germanium.
Silicon has better temperature stability than germanium.
Silicon is used in integrated circuits.
Silicon is used in solar cells.
Silicon is used in diodes.
Silicon is used in transistors.
Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth’s crust.
The atomic number of germanium is 32.
Germanium has 4 valence electrons.
Germanium has a band gap of approximately 0.7 eV.
Germanium has a smaller band gap than silicon.
Germanium has higher leakage current at high temperature.
The first transistors and diodes used germanium.
Germanium has limited present use.
Germanium is used in special high-frequency applications.
Germanium is used in infrared applications.
Germanium is more temperature-sensitive than silicon.
Semiconductor conductivity increases with a rise in temperature.
Semiconductor resistivity decreases with a rise in temperature.
Semiconductor resistance decreases with a rise in temperature.
More covalent bonds break when semiconductor temperature rises.
Breaking more covalent bonds produces more free electrons and holes.
Semiconductor temperature behaviour is opposite to that of metals.
Intrinsic carrier concentration increases exponentially with temperature.
Pure semiconductor resistance decreases as temperature increases.
A pure semiconductor has high resistance at 0 K.
A pure semiconductor acts as an insulator at 0 K.
A doped semiconductor has lower resistance than an intrinsic semiconductor.
Semiconductors have a negative temperature coefficient of resistance.
The resistance of a semiconductor falls with a rise in temperature.
Metals have a positive temperature coefficient of resistance.
Doping is the controlled addition of impurity atoms to a pure semiconductor.
The purpose of doping is to increase conductivity in a controlled manner.
The dopant concentration is very small.
The dopant concentration can be one impurity atom in 10⁶ to 10⁸ atoms.
Donor doping produces n-type semiconductors.
Acceptor doping produces p-type semiconductors.
Doping produces an extrinsic semiconductor.
Electrons are the majority carriers in an n-type semiconductor.
Holes are the minority carriers in an n-type semiconductor.
An n-type dopant is pentavalent.
Pentavalent dopants belong to Group 15.
Phosphorus is an n-type dopant.
Arsenic is an n-type dopant.
Antimony is an n-type dopant.
The extra electron from an n-type dopant becomes a free electron.
The extra electron makes the dopant a donor.
An n-type semiconductor is overall electrically neutral.
Positive ions balance the extra electrons in an n-type semiconductor.
Holes are the majority carriers in a p-type semiconductor.
Electrons are the minority carriers in a p-type semiconductor.
A p-type dopant is trivalent.
Trivalent dopants belong to Group 13.
Boron is a p-type dopant.
Aluminium is a p-type dopant.
Gallium is a p-type dopant.
Indium is a p-type dopant.
The deficiency caused by a p-type dopant creates a hole.
The p-type dopant is an acceptor.
A p-type semiconductor is overall electrically neutral.
Negative ions balance the holes in a p-type semiconductor.
An intrinsic semiconductor has equal numbers of electrons and holes.
Electrons are the majority charge carriers in an n-type semiconductor.
Electrons are the minority charge carriers in a p-type semiconductor.
Conduction occurs through free electrons in the conduction band.
An electron has negative charge.
Electrons provide the main conduction in an n-type semiconductor.
A hole is a vacancy of an electron in a covalent bond.
A hole acts as a positive charge carrier.
The number of holes in an intrinsic semiconductor equals the number of electrons.
Holes are the majority charge carriers in a p-type semiconductor.
Holes are the minority charge carriers in an n-type semiconductor.
The apparent movement of holes is opposite to the movement of electrons.
The full form of transistor is transfer resistor.
A transistor works by current amplification or switching using two p-n junctions.
The two types of transistors are n-p-n and p-n-p.
The emitter of a transistor is heavily doped.
The base of a transistor is thin and lightly doped.
The collector of a transistor is moderately doped.
The emitter-base junction is forward biased.
The collector-base junction is reverse biased.
A small input current controls a large output current in a transistor.
A transistor amplifier increases the strength of weak signals.
A transistor switch provides ON/OFF control in digital circuits.
A transistor oscillator generates oscillating signals.
Transistors are basic building blocks of integrated circuits in computers and mobile devices.
Transistors are used for signal processing in radios and televisions.
Transistors are used for switching high-power loads in power control.
A rectifier converts AC to DC.
A rectifier can be half-wave or full-wave.
LED stands for Light Emitting Diode.
LEDs are used in indicators.
LEDs are used in displays.
LEDs are used in lighting.
A Zener diode is used for voltage regulation.
A photodiode is used for light detection.
Photodiodes are used in solar cells.
A solar cell converts light to electricity.
A diode can be used for fast switching in circuits.
Clipping and clamping are used in wave-shaping circuits.
A varactor provides voltage-controlled capacitance.
A superconductor has zero electrical resistance below its critical temperature.
A superconductor exhibits perfect diamagnetism.
The Meissner effect expels the magnetic field.
The critical temperature is the temperature below which superconductivity appears.
Superconductivity is destroyed above the critical magnetic field.
The critical current density is the maximum current density a superconductor can carry.
Mercury is an example of a superconductor with a critical temperature of 4.2 K.
Niobium alloys are examples of superconductors.
High-Tc cuprates are examples of superconductors.
YBCO is a high-Tc cuprate superconductor.
Superconductors are used in MRI magnets.
Superconductors are used in Maglev trains.
Superconductors are used for future lossless power transmission.
Superconductors are used in SQUIDs.

16.text: The SI unit of electric charge is the coulomb (C).
Electric charge is also measured in esu and emu.
The elementary charge is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
One coulomb is the charge of 6.25 × 10¹⁸ electrons.
The SI unit of electric current is the ampere (A).
One ampere equals one coulomb per second (1 A = 1 C/s).
Small currents are measured in mA and μA.
The conventional direction of current is from positive to negative.
The direction of electron flow is from negative to positive.
The SI unit of potential difference or voltage is the volt (V).
One volt equals one joule per coulomb (1 V = 1 J/C).
The SI unit of emf is the volt (V).
The SI unit of resistance is the ohm (Ω).
One ohm equals one volt per ampere (1 Ω = 1 V/A).
High resistance is measured in kΩ and MΩ.
The SI unit of resistivity is the ohm-metre (Ω m).
Resistivity is also measured in Ω cm.
The SI unit of conductivity is the siemens per metre (S/m).
Conductivity equals the reciprocal of resistivity (σ = 1/ρ).
The SI unit of conductance is the siemens (S).
Conductance equals the reciprocal of resistance (G = 1/R).
The older unit of conductance is the mho.
The resistance of metals increases when temperature rises.
The resistance of semiconductors decreases when temperature rises.
Nichrome and Constantan alloys show very small change in resistance when temperature rises.
The resistance of electrolytes decreases when temperature rises.
The resistance of superconductors becomes zero below the critical temperature.
Conductors have very low resistivity.
Silver, copper, and aluminium are examples of conductors.
Alloys have higher resistivity than pure metals.
Nichrome, Constantan, and Manganin are examples of alloys.
Semiconductors have intermediate resistivity.
Silicon and germanium are examples of semiconductors.
Insulators have very high resistivity.
Rubber, glass, and plastic are examples of insulators.
Silver is the best conductor because it has the lowest resistivity.
The current through all components in a series connection is the same.
Current divides in a parallel connection.
The current division in a parallel connection is inversely proportional to resistance.
Kirchhoff’s first law states that the sum of currents at a junction is zero.
Voltage divides in a series connection.
The voltage in a series connection is V = V₁ + V₂ + …
The voltage across all components in a parallel connection is the same.
Kirchhoff’s second law states that the sum of voltage drops in a closed loop is zero.
The SI unit of power is the watt (W).
The commercial units of power are kW and MW.
One kilowatt equals 1000 watts (1 kW = 1000 W).
One horsepower equals 746 watts (1 hp = 746 W).
One kilowatt-hour is the energy consumed by a 1 kW device in 1 hour.
One kilowatt-hour equals 3.6 × 10⁶ joules.
One unit of electricity equals 1 kWh.
The board definition of one unit is energy equivalent to 1 kWh.
Electricity cost is charged per unit (kWh).
Electric heating is used in electric irons, heaters, geysers, and toasters.
Incandescent bulbs are used for old-style lighting.
Electric stoves and induction devices are used for cooking.
Electric fuses are used for protection.
Electric furnaces and welding use the heating effect of current industrially.
Electric motors use the magnetic effect of current.
Fans, pumps, and electric vehicles use motors.
Generators are used in power stations.
Electromagnets are used in cranes, relays, and MRI.
Galvanometers, ammeters, and voltmeters are measuring instruments using the magnetic effect.
Loudspeakers and microphones are used for communication.
Magnetic tapes and hard disks are older storage applications of the magnetic effect.
The working principle of an electric fuse is the heating effect of current.
Fuse material is a low-melting-point alloy of tin and lead.
A fuse melts when current exceeds its rated value.
A melted fuse breaks the circuit.
A fuse is connected in series with the device or circuit.
Overcurrent protection prevents damage due to excess current.
A fuse melts immediately during a short circuit.
The main fuse and individual circuit fuses are used in household wiring.
Some appliances have built-in fuses.
A fuse protects wiring from overheating and fire.
Earthing prevents electric shock.
Earthing provides a low-resistance path to ground for leakage current.
Earthing keeps the metal body of an appliance at zero potential.
During a fault condition, excess current flows to earth and the fuse blows.
The colour code for an earthing wire is green or green-yellow.
A short circuit occurs when live and neutral wires touch each other directly.
Insulation failure can cause a short circuit.
Overloading occurs when too many high-power devices are used.
Overloading produces very high current, causing heating and fire hazard.
Fuse or MCB and proper earthing prevent overloading hazards.
The working principle of a generator is electromagnetic induction, according to Faraday’s law.
A generator produces induced emf when magnetic flux changes.
The components of a generator include an armature, field magnets, slip rings or a commutator, and brushes.
The types of generators are AC generators (alternators) and DC generators.
A generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
The input energy of a generator is mechanical energy from rotation.
The output energy of a generator is electrical energy.
In a generator, a coil rotates in a magnetic field and produces induced emf and current.
The working principle of a motor is the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, according to Fleming’s Left Hand Rule.
A current-carrying coil experiences torque in a magnetic field.
The components of a motor include an armature, magnets, a commutator, and brushes.
A motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy.
The input energy of a motor is electrical energy.
The output energy of a motor is mechanical energy from rotation.
A motor process converts electrical energy into torque and then rotation.
The working principle of a transformer is mutual induction.
A transformer requires alternating current with changing flux.
The construction of a transformer includes a primary coil, secondary coil, and soft iron core.
An AC transformer works because changing flux induces emf.
A DC transformer does not work because there is no change in flux after the initial moment.
Mutual induction requires a varying magnetic field.
A rectifier converts AC into DC.
A diode is used as the device in a rectifier.
Rectifiers include half-wave and full-wave types.
The types of rectifiers are half-wave, full-wave, and bridge rectifiers.
Rectifiers are used in power supplies and chargers.
An inverter converts DC into AC.
Inverters are used in UPS systems, solar power systems, and battery backup.
An inverter produces alternating voltage for AC appliances.
Generators are an application of electromagnetic induction for power generation.
Transformers are an application of electromagnetic induction for voltage conversion.
Induction cooktops use electromagnetic induction for heating.
Wireless charging uses electromagnetic induction for mobile phones and electric vehicles.
Magnetic brakes in trains use electromagnetic induction.
Dynamic microphones use electromagnetic induction.
Induction motors use electromagnetic induction in industrial motors.
Metal detectors use electromagnetic induction.

14.text: An unbalanced force changes the state of motion by accelerating, decelerating, or changing direction.
A balanced force causes no change in the state of motion.
An object under a balanced force remains at rest or moves with uniform velocity.
A frictional force opposes relative motion or the tendency of motion.
A gravitational force attracts objects towards each other.
Weight is associated with gravitational force.
A centripetal force keeps an object in a circular path towards the centre.
A tension force pulls along a string or rope.
A normal force is a perpendicular push by a surface.
A spring force is a restoring force described by Hooke’s law.
The SI unit of force is the newton (N).
Other units of force include the dyne, kilogram-force (kgf), and poundal.
One newton equals one kilogram metre per second squared (1 N = 1 kg m s⁻²).
One newton equals 10⁵ dynes.
The SI unit of weight is the newton (N).
Another unit of weight is the kilogram-force (kgf).
One kilogram-force is approximately 9.8 newtons.
Newton’s first law is also called the law of inertia.
Seat belts are an application of Newton’s first law.
The effects of sudden braking demonstrate Newton’s first law.
The statement that objects at rest stay at rest is an application of Newton’s first law.
Newton’s second law is expressed as F = ma.
Vehicle design is an application of Newton’s second law.
Calculating the acceleration of rockets or lifts is an application of Newton’s second law.
Newton’s third law is the law of action and reaction.
Rocket propulsion is an application of Newton’s third law.
Walking is an application of Newton’s third law.
Swimming is an application of Newton’s third law.
Gun recoil is an application of Newton’s third law.
Jet engines are an application of Newton’s third law.
A passenger lurches forward when a bus stops suddenly, demonstrating Newton’s first law.
A book remains on a table until pushed, demonstrating Newton’s first law.
A heavier suitcase needs more force to accelerate, demonstrating Newton’s second law.
Pushing an empty cart versus a loaded cart demonstrates Newton’s second law.
Rocket gases push down and the rocket moves up, demonstrating Newton’s third law.
During walking, the foot pushes the ground backward.
During walking, the ground pushes the foot forward.
A gun recoils when a bullet is fired.
The foot pushes the ground backward and the ground pushes the foot forward.
A rocket expels gases downward.
The gases push the rocket upward.
A gun pushes a bullet forward.
A bullet pushes a gun backward, causing recoil.
A bird pushes air downward.
The air pushes the bird upward.
A swimmer pushes water backward.
The water pushes the swimmer forward.
A hammer hits a nail.
The nail hits the hammer with equal force.
The Earth pulls an apple downward.
The apple pulls the Earth upward.
The apple produces a very small acceleration of the Earth.
The total linear momentum of an isolated system is conserved if there is no external force.
The total momentum before a collision equals the total momentum after the collision.
Total momentum is conserved for collisions of any type.
The total momentum of an explosion remains zero if the system is initially at rest.
The momentum of the gun-and-bullet system is conserved during recoil.
The momentum of the rocket-and-exhaust-gases system is conserved.
During rocket propulsion, exhaust gases gain backward momentum.
During rocket propulsion, the rocket gains forward momentum.
The forward momentum of a bullet equals the backward momentum of the gun during recoil.
Vehicle safety design uses the principles of collisions.
Airbags increase the time of impact and decrease the force.
Catching a ball by drawing the hands back increases the time interval.
Jet engines use high-speed exhaust to produce a large momentum change.
The SI unit of work is the joule (J).
Other units of work include the erg, electronvolt (eV), calorie, and kilowatt-hour (kWh).
One joule equals one newton metre (1 J = 1 N m).
One joule equals one kilogram metre squared per second squared (1 J = 1 kg m² s⁻²).
One joule equals 10⁷ ergs.
One electronvolt equals 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ joules.
Kinetic energy has translational and rotational forms.
Potential energy has gravitational, elastic, electric, chemical, and nuclear forms.
Mechanical energy equals kinetic energy plus potential energy.
Thermal or heat energy is internal energy due to molecular motion.
Other forms of energy include sound, light, electrical, magnetic, and nuclear energy.
A generator or dynamo converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
An electric motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy.
A battery or cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy.
An LED or bulb converts electrical energy into light energy.
A solar cell converts light energy into electrical energy.
A nuclear power plant converts nuclear energy into heat and then electrical energy.
Free fall is an example of potential energy converting into kinetic energy.
A pendulum is an example of potential energy converting into kinetic energy.
A roller coaster is an example of potential energy converting into kinetic energy.
Friction in brakes converts kinetic energy into heat.
The law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed.
Mechanical energy conservation is expressed as KE + PE = constant when only conservative forces act.
A pendulum demonstrates mechanical energy conservation.
Free fall demonstrates mechanical energy conservation.
A spring-mass system demonstrates mechanical energy conservation.
Ideal collisions demonstrate mechanical energy conservation.
The SI unit of power is the watt (W).
Other units of power include horsepower (hp), kilowatt (kW), and megawatt (MW).
One watt equals one joule per second (1 W = 1 J s⁻¹).
One horsepower equals 746 watts.
Static friction opposes the tendency of motion.
Static friction is self-adjusting.
The maximum static friction is μₛN.
Kinetic or sliding friction opposes actual sliding motion.
Kinetic or sliding friction is μₖN.
Rolling friction opposes rolling.
Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction.
Fluid friction or viscous drag opposes motion in fluids.
Friction is necessary for forward push during walking or running.
Friction provides grip between a pen and paper during writing.
Braking of vehicles converts kinetic energy into heat through friction.
Frictional grip prevents objects from slipping when they are held.
Friction produces heat to ignite a matchstick.
Friction enables power transmission in belts and pulleys.
Friction enables walking because without friction people slip.
Friction allows vehicles to move and stop through traction and braking.
Friction helps in writing and holding through grip.
Friction produces heat in matchsticks and during drilling.
Friction enables power transmission through belt drives.
Friction causes wear and tear in machine parts and tyres.
Friction produces unwanted heat, causing overheating of engines and brakes.
Friction reduces efficiency by causing energy loss in machines.
Friction opposes motion and causes extra fuel consumption in vehicles.
Friction makes surfaces rough over time.
Centripetal force is a real force towards the centre.
Centripetal force provides the necessary acceleration for circular motion.
Centrifugal force is a pseudo force in a rotating frame.
Centrifugal force acts away from the centre.
Tension can provide centripetal force.
Gravity can provide centripetal force.
Friction can provide centripetal force.
Electrostatic force can provide centripetal force.
Magnetic force can provide centripetal force.
Friction provides centripetal force for a vehicle on a level circular road.
The component of normal force plus friction provides centripetal force for a vehicle on a banked road.
Gravitational force provides centripetal force in satellite or planetary motion.
Tension provides centripetal force for a stone tied to a string.
Electrostatic attraction provides centripetal force for an electron around a nucleus.
Gravity plus normal force provides centripetal force in a loop-the-loop.
Water is thrown outward in a washing machine because of centrifugal force.
Mud flies off a rotating wheel because of centrifugal force.
Particles move outward in a rotating frame because of centrifugal force.
The feeling of being pushed outward in a merry-go-round is caused by pseudo force.
A centrifuge separates cream or blood using centrifugal force.
Denser particles move outward in a centrifuge.
Planetary rings and the shape of the Earth demonstrate outward effects associated with centrifugal force.
The Earth bulges at the equator.
A lever is used in scissors, see-saws, crowbars, bottle openers, and the human forearm.
An inclined plane is used in ramps, slopes, screws, and wedges.
A pulley is used for lifting heavy loads with cranes, flagpoles, and elevators.
A wheel and axle is used in steering wheels, door knobs, and screwdrivers.
A screw jack is used for lifting cars or heavy vehicles.
Gears are used in bicycles, clocks, and automobiles.
Gears provide speed or torque conversion.

19.text: Sound requires a material medium.
The material medium for sound can be a solid, liquid, or gas.
Sound cannot travel in a vacuum.
Sound is a mechanical wave.
Sound is a longitudinal wave.
Sound propagates through compressions and rarefactions.
The general speed order of sound is solid > liquid > gas.
The approximate speed of sound in air at 20–25°C is 340–343 m/s.
The approximate speed of sound in water at 20–25°C is 1480–1500 m/s.
The approximate speed of sound in steel or iron at 20–25°C is 5000–6000 m/s.
The approximate speed of sound in glass at 20–25°C is 5000–6000 m/s.
The speed of sound in a vacuum is zero.
Sound cannot travel in a vacuum.
Frequency is the number of vibrations per second.
Frequency is the number of compressions per second.
The unit of frequency is hertz (Hz).
Frequency determines the pitch of sound.
The human audible frequency range is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
Wavelength is the distance between two successive compressions or rarefactions.
Higher frequency corresponds to smaller wavelength.
At a sound speed of 340 m/s in air, a frequency of 20 Hz has a wavelength of 17 m.
At a sound speed of 340 m/s in air, a frequency of 20 kHz has a wavelength of 1.7 cm.
Amplitude is the maximum displacement of particles from their mean position.
Amplitude determines the loudness of sound.
Amplitude determines the intensity of sound.
The energy of sound is proportional to the square of its amplitude.
The unit of amplitude is metre (m).
Amplitude has no effect on the speed of sound.
Amplitude has no effect on frequency.
Amplitude has no effect on pitch.
Pitch is directly proportional to frequency.
Higher frequency produces higher pitch.
Low frequency produces a bass or deep sound.
A male voice is an example of a bass or deep sound.
High frequency produces a shrill sound.
A female voice is an example of a shrill sound.
A whistle is an example of a shrill sound.
Pitch is the sensation of frequency in the brain.
Pitch is independent of amplitude or loudness.
Loudness is directly related to amplitude.
Higher amplitude produces a louder sound.
Loudness is the sensation of intensity or amplitude.
The unit of loudness is decibel (dB).
Loudness is independent of frequency or pitch.
Quality or timbre distinguishes two sounds having the same pitch and loudness.
Quality or timbre depends on the waveform present.
Quality or timbre depends on the overtones present.
Quality or timbre depends on the harmonics present.
